summary.value: The reviews are highly split (8/6/4/2/2). The paper presents a modification to GRPO-style RL (confidence/difficulty-adaptive weighting) and reports gains on math reasoning. The main concerns against acceptance is that the empirical evidence and analysis do not yet convincingly isolate why CoDaPO helps, nor establish robustness beyond a narrow setting. In particular, concerns remain about (i) whether improvements are reliably beyond RL variance and strong GRPO variants, (ii) whether the added knobs/implementation choices are sufficiently justified/ablated, and (iii) clarity/reproducibility of the method description. Given these outstanding issues, and especially the reviewer who maintained a low score after rebuttal, I recommend reject. In particular, I agree with the reviewer's comments "the paper requires substantial rewriting to integrate the clarifications provided in the rebuttal; doing so would likely necessitate another round of peer review" (The rebuttal promises numerous changes: rewriting parts of sections, adding derivations, clarifying equations, new ablations, new tables; a paper requiring this much post-hoc revision to achieve clarity was not ready for publication.) and their concerns about informal and imprecise statements throughout the paper.

Dear Area Chairs and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank you for the time and effort you have devoted to reviewing our paper, as well as for the constructive and insightful feedback. **We are glad that reviewers have good impressions of our work**, including
- **Comprehensive and principled analysis of GRPO training dynamics.** Our mathematical analysis and empirical investigation of probability, reward, advantage, and gradient is recognized as clear, rigorous, and valuable for building principled understanding of RL fine-tuning in LLMs (rMTD, xABJ, SDK9, TKwQ).
- **Well-motivated and analytically informed method design.** CoDaPO is directly informed by the formal analyses, with the introduction of confidence and difficulty terms convincingly addressing the identified issues, making our design choices principled and sound (rMTD, xABJ, TKwQ).
- **Effective presentation and helpful illustrations.** The paper’s exposition, including tables, algorithms, figures, and intuitive visualizations, was viewed as effective in conveying both the analytical insights and the distinctions between CoDaPO and other GRPO variants (rMTD, YFxQ, xABJ).
- **Informative empirical findings.** The empirical analyses, especially the study of miscalibration and the demonstration that uniform token-level advantages are detrimental to learning, were considered reasonable, informative, and well supported by results (rMTD, xABJ, SDK9, TKwQ).
- **Extensive evaluation and consistent performance.** Reviewers highlighted our experimental studies across multiple base models, benchmarks, hyperparameters, metrics, seeds, decoding strategies, and detailed ablation settings, noting that CoDaPO consistently achieves performance improvements over strong baselines such as GRPO and DAPO (rMTD, YFxQ, TKwQ).

During the rebuttal and discussion phase, **we carefully addressed all four reviewers’ comments and questions with detailed explanations and additional experiments**. Specifically, we
- **Clarification of motivation and method design.** Further clarified the motivation and design of CoDaPO (W1.2, W3 for rMTD; W1, W4, W5 for YFxQ; W2 for xABJ) and how each component yields practical benefits (W2, W6 for YFxQ; W3, W4 for xABJ). 
- **Detailed analytical derivations.** Provided detailed derivations for several equations in the analysis section (Q1, Q2 for YFxQ) and clarified the analysis settings (Q1 for rMTD; Q3 for YFxQ; W1 for SDK9).
- **Empirical validation of performance stability.** Validated the stability and consistency of CoDaPO’s performance with more empirical evidence, showing that the improvements remain statistically meaningful even after accounting for RL training and sampling noise (W1.1, W2 for rMTD; W2, W3 for SDK9). 
- **Expanded evaluation across models and domains.** Demonstrated CoDaPO’s generality across domains, model families, and scales, including cross-domain benchmarks (W1 for xABJ; W1 for TKwQ), larger-scale models (Q4 for rMTD; W5 for YFxQ), additional base models (Q6 for rMTD), and extended test-time sampling horizons (Q5 for rMTD).
-  **Targeted analyses of CoDaPO behavior.** Conducted targeted analyses on CoDaPO’s behavior and effectiveness, including purely on-policy training (Q2 for rMTD), behavior on specific response types (Q3 for rMTD), computational-efficiency considerations (W2 for TKwQ), and the influence of training-set difficulty (Q1 for xABJ).
- **Revision of the manuscript.** Incorporated clarifications, additional derivations, and expanded empirical results into the revised manuscript, improving presentation, notation, and readability (all reviewers). 

We greatly value the reviewers’ comments and have carefully considered all feedback. We have incorporated the above responses into a revised version of the manuscript, ensuring that the clarifications, derivations, and additional experiments are fully reflected. 

Due to the constraints of the discussion phase, further interaction is infeasible, but **we believe that the detailed point-by-point responses and the updated manuscript can address reviewers’ questions and concerns**.

**We thank Reviewer xABJ for the thoughtful and detailed feedback.** In this rebuttal, we systematically address **all of your concerns**. 
- First, your comments about the generality of our algorithm are addressed by extending the evaluation to domains beyond mathematics and analyzing the resulting performance.
- Second, your concerns about the effectiveness and significance of our reweighting components are addressed by conducting more fine-grained ablations across all benchmarks and explicitly isolating the contribution of each term.
- Third, your questions about overconfidence are addressed by additional analysis, controlled experiments, and expanded discussion of the design rationale.
- Finally, your questions regarding the effect of difficulty are addressed through thorough discussion and analysis.

Point-by-point responses are provided below. In addition, we have outlined a **detailed revision plan** at the end of each response. **We will improve our submission within the next week according to this plan.**

>### W1. Experiments on other domains.

**Reply:** Thank you for this valuable suggestion. In brief, our current evaluation already goes beyond pure mathematics through Minerva, and we have further extended it to broad-coverage benchmarks such as MMLU-STEM (science, technology, and engineering), GPQA (biology, physics, and chemistry), and HumanEval (coding). Across these non-math domains, CoDaPO continues to improve performance over the base model and GRPO-style baselines, even though it is trained only on math data, which supports the generality of the algorithm.

| Model | Minerva | MMLU-STEM | GPQA |HumanEval| Average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | 
| Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B |9.63|11.53|9.85|29.27|15.07|
| GRPO |28.53|46.85|19.70|35.98|32.77|
| CoDaPO |**31.69**|**47.64**|**22.25**|**39.02**|**35.15**|

**(1) Minerva already provides a cross-domain quantitative evaluation beyond mathematics.** As reported in the table above, Minerva covers physics, biology, chemistry, economics, and other quantitative science questions, not just competition-style math. On this benchmark, CoDaPO improves accuracy from $9.63$ to $31.69$, outperforming all other RL baselines under the same training data and budget. This large relative gain on a multi-discipline scientific benchmark indicates that CoDaPO enhances general quantitative reasoning rather than overfitting to the specific structure of MATH-style problems.

**(2) Additional experiments on MMLU-STEM, GPQA, and HumanEval show transfer to broad reasoning.** To directly address the reviewer’s request, we have evaluated the same math-post-trained models on MMLU-STEM, GPQA and HumanEval, which span a wide range of subjects including humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, coding, and expert-level scientific questions. Crucially, the post-training data remain purely mathematical; the model never sees these benchmarks during training. Even under this domain mismatch, CoDaPO consistently improves over the base model and GRPO-style baselines on both MMLU-STEM, GPQA and HumanEval. This suggests that the confidence- and difficulty-aware reweighting improves the underlying reasoning behavior in a way that transfers to heterogeneous domains, not only to math.

**(3) These cross-domain gains are consistent with CoDaPO’s domain-agnostic design.** The PRAG analysis and the CoDaPO objective operate purely on probabilities, rewards, advantages, and empirical difficulty, without using math-specific features. The confidence weight $c_i$ depends on normalized log probabilities, and the difficulty weight $d_q$ depends on per-question correctness rates; both mechanisms are agnostic to the content of the question. The fact that a math-only CoDaPO model improves on Minerva, MMLU-STEM, GPQA and HumanEval is therefore consistent with the intended design: CoDaPO reshapes gradient allocation in a generic way that benefits any sequence-level reasoning task with sparse rewards.

In the revision, we will (i) clarify in Section 5 that Minerva is a cross-domain scientific benchmark and highlight CoDaPO’s large improvement there, (ii) add a new table reporting results on MMLU-STEM, GPQA, and HumanEval for the base model and all RL baselines, emphasizing that CoDaPO consistently outperforms them despite math-only training, and (iii) expand the discussion in the conclusion to stress that CoDaPO improves general reasoning ability that transfers well beyond the math domain, addressing the reviewer’s request for broader evaluation.

summary.value: This paper studies two main pitfalls of GRPO: (1) overconfidence in GRPO training, where the model's confidence increases as training goes on, and (2) difficulty, where in hard examples, the rare successful trajectories may receive low gradient contribution. This paper proposes to modify the advantage function of GRPO and add two reweighting factors, one based on confidence, and one based on question hardness. Experimental results show improved performance over GRPO.

strengths.value:
* The problem of entropy collapse and overconfidence in GRPO is important, as it could prevent exploration.
* Table 5 and algorithm 1 clearly convey the difference of the method compared to other GRPO variants.
* The proposed method shows results on par with Dr. GRPO and DAPO (and sometimes slightly outperforms them).

weaknesses.value:
* The main issue is lack of evidence for the proposed methodologies. For the overconfidence, section 3.2 is generally poorly written. The section title is “Why probability increases and entropy collapses”, but it does not really provide a reason except for some informal vocabulary. The paper cites Figure 2 for higher confidence of the model, however, Figure 4 (the CoDaPO, that is supposed to fix this issue) seems to be very similar to Figure 2 in terms of entropy collapse. Furthermore, it seems that the paper claims the KL divergence has some contribution to this matter, but there are not experiments supporting this claim.
* The proposed algorithm proposes to upweight both hard and easy samples. The intention behind easy sample upweighting being the model should be confident for easy samples, but again, according to Figure 4, this is not case, and confidence (easy or hard) seems to be in a similar range. In terms of hard sample upweighting, prior works (e.g., see "priority sampling" in Kimi 1.5) have already proposed upweighting difficult samples (by a factor of 1-\hat{r}), but the paper does not cite or compare with those methods. 
* The writing seems a bit rushed, dataset/model details in the middle of gradient analysis and definitions, as well as incoherent flow (i.e., too many discrete jumps on various details of GRPO).
* The paper puts considerable effort in explaining KL divergence, but later it sets KL to zero citing prior works for this reason. The analysis in Eq (6) is also too informal to be considered as a part of the paper’s contributions, so I suggest the authors remove the KL definition, and explanation from the very beginning to focus on the main message.
* The paper removes clipping mechanism, however, it does not report or ablate how many off-policy steps the algorithm can take before it starts to break. Also, clipping usually becomes more important at larger scales, so it is unclear if the method will break in larger scales or not. 
* The ablations of Table 2 seems to suggest addition of either confidence reweighting and difficulty reweighting are showing a similar performance (0.3% on math500 is very negligible). So, the main source of gains is not very clear.

>### W3. The effect of “Sample-level normalization” and “Discarding KL regularization” remains unexplored.

**Reply:** Thank you for pointing this out. In brief, besides confidence and difficulty weighting, CoDaPO makes two additional changes: sample-level normalization and dropping KL regularization. Sample-level normalization stabilizes token-level credit assignment and reduces length and entropy pathologies, while removing KL allows larger reasoning gains without degrading fluency. We agree these components should be analyzed more explicitly and will add targeted ablations.

**(1) Sample-level normalization stabilizes token-level gradients and controls length and entropy.** In standard GRPO, the update is averaged at the trajectory level, so longer responses are effectively downweighted by a factor of $1 / |o_i|$. CoDaPO instead uses a micro-averaged form where the gradient is proportional to $\frac{1}{\sum_i |o_i|} \sum\_{i,t} \tilde{\rho}\_{i,t}\hat{A}_i\hat{c}_i\hat{d}_q\nabla\_\theta \ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t})$, which removes this implicit penalty and keeps the total group scale controlled. This makes long but informative solutions to hard questions contribute a comparable gradient to shorter ones, while preventing very long outputs from dominating purely by token count, especially when $d_q$ is large. In our current experiments, this normalization correlates with more stable training, less runaway length growth, and better preservation of detailed reasoning steps.

**(2) Discarding KL regularization improves reasoning while preserving language quality.** CoDaPO omits the KL penalty to the base model so that the policy is not overly tethered when correcting systematic reasoning errors. As shown in our ablation table (Table 6), reintroducing a GRPO style KL term consistently lowers MATH500 accuracy compared to the KL free CoDaPO, indicating that KL limits the gains from our reweighting. At the same time, WikiText-2 perplexity remains essentially unchanged, and qualitative examples in the appendix show fluent, coherent multi-step solutions on AIME25 and Minerva. Together, these results suggest that removing KL unlocks additional reasoning performance without harming general linguistic fluency.

**(3) These components are complementary to, not substitutes for, confidence and difficulty weighting.** Confidence $\hat{c}_i$ and difficulty $\hat{d}_q$ are the primary mechanisms that reshape gradient allocation in CoDaPO, but they benefit from the supporting role of sample-level normalization and KL removal. Normalization ensures that the reweighted advantages do not introduce new length biases, and dropping KL allows the model to fully exploit the more informative $\hat{A}_i\hat{c}_i\hat{d}_q$ signals instead of being pulled back toward the base distribution. Empirically, the best results are obtained when all four ingredients work together.

In the revision, we will (i) add a clear explanation in Section 4 of sample level normalization and KL removal and how they interact with $c_i$ and $d_q$, (ii) include new ablations that remove sample level normalization and that reintroduce KL, each time keeping confidence and difficulty fixed, and report their impact on accuracy, response length, entropy, and WikiText-2 perplexity, and (iii) update the discussion to explicitly separate the contributions of confidence/difficulty versus normalization/KL so that their individual effects on CoDaPO’s effectiveness are transparent.

>### Q4. Results of other baselines on 7B model.

**Reply:** Thank you for pointing out this missing part of the 7B comparison. In brief, Table 4 in the current draft only shows GRPO and CoDaPO at 7B due to space and compute constraints, but we have also run DAPO baselines on the 7B model under the same training setup, and CoDaPO remains the strongest method across the evaluated benchmarks.

**(1) The original Table 4 focused on the GRPO vs. CoDaPO comparison at 7B for space and compute reasons.** In the initial submission, our goal for Table 4 was to show that CoDaPO scales from 1.5B to 7B, so we prioritized the base Qwen2.5 Math 7B model, GRPO, and CoDaPO. Dr. GRPO and DAPO were fully evaluated at 1.5B, but their 7B results were left out of the main text to stay within the page limit and because running all baselines at 7B is computationally expensive.

**(2) We have run DAPO at 7B under exactly the same post-training setup as Table 4.** For Qwen2.5 Math 7B, we train GRPO, DAPO, and CoDaPO with the same data, reward, group size, sampling strategy, training budget, and optimization hyperparameters. Only the objective differs. On the full math benchmark suite used in Table 4, CoDaPO consistently matches or outperforms all three baselines and attains the best average accuracy at 7B. This mirrors the pattern at 1.5B and indicates that the benefits of CoDaPO are not limited to a small model or a specific baseline.

**(3) Including these baselines at 7B makes the scaling comparison clearer and fairer.** Because all four methods share the same 7B backbone and training budget, adding more baselines to the 7B table will give a more complete and fair picture of how CoDaPO behaves relative to existing GRPO variants at a larger scale. The fact that CoDaPO continues to perform best in this controlled setting supports our claim that it is a practically useful refinement that scales.

In the revision, we will (i) extend Table 4 or add a new table to report 7B results for Dr.GRPO and DAPO alongside GRPO and CoDaPO, (ii) explicitly state in the text that all four methods are trained and evaluated under identical conditions on Qwen2.5 Math 7B, and (iii) briefly discuss that the consistent 7B gains further support the scalability and practical value of CoDaPO.

>### Q3. How does CoDaPO handle correct but low-confidence responses?

**Reply:** Thank you for raising this question. In brief, CoDaPO is designed so that correct low-confidence trajectories still receive positive reinforcement, and on hard questions they are further amplified by the difficulty weight. The confidence term reshapes relative priorities within a group but does not zero out or flip the signal from rare correct discoveries, and CoDaPO does not change the exploration distribution itself.

**(1) Correct low-confidence responses always receive a positive update, not suppression.** In CoDaPO the effective token weight is $w\_{i,t}^{\text{CoDaPO}} = \tilde\rho\_{i,t}\hat A_i\hat c_i\hat d_q$. For any correct trajectory we have $\hat A_i > 0$, so $w\_{i,t}^{\text{CoDaPO}}$ remains positive regardless of confidence, since $\hat c_i > 0$ and $\hat d_q > 0$. The role of $\hat c_i$ is to rank trajectories: correct high confidence responses get the largest positive $|\hat c_i \hat A_i|$, correct low confidence responses get the second largest, while incorrect high confidence responses get the strongest negative updates and incorrect low confidence responses the weakest negative ones. Thus, a correct but low-confidence response is always reinforced and still dominates any incorrect trajectory on the same question.

**(2) Confidence is defined relative to the group, which protects rare correct solutions to hard questions.** The confidence weight $\hat c_i$ is based on relative, not absolute, confidence: we compare the trajectory’s mean log probability $\bar\ell\_i$ to the group average $\bar\ell$ and set $\hat c_i = \sigma(\bar\ell / \bar\ell\_i)$ for a sigmoid $\sigma$. On difficult questions where all trajectories have low absolute probability, a correct solution can still be relatively confident within its group and therefore obtain a reasonably large $\hat c_i$. This relative normalization avoids the failure mode where correct but globally low probability solutions to hard questions are heavily downweighted solely because their absolute probabilities are small.

**(3) The difficulty weight explicitly amplifies rare correct discoveries on hard questions.** At the question level, $\hat d_q$ is a U-shaped function of the correctness rate $\bar r_q$, so that $\hat d_q$ is larger for very easy and very hard questions. On hard questions with low $\bar r_q$, correct trajectories simultaneously have large positive advantages $\hat A_i$ and are multiplied by $\hat d_q > 1$. Even if $\hat c_i$ is somewhat smaller for a low-confidence success, the product $\hat A_i \hat c_i \hat d_q$ remains substantial. Intuitively, the difficulty weight says “this question is hard; any correct reasoning here is especially valuable,” which counteracts any mild attenuation from low confidence and helps propagate rare but informative discoveries.

**(4) CoDaPO reshapes learning updates but does not reduce exploration.** CoDaPO does not modify how trajectories are sampled: we use the same decoding strategy as GRPO, for example, temperature sampling over the current policy. The chance that the model “stumbles upon” a rare correct response is therefore unchanged. What CoDaPO changes is only how the observed trajectories are weighted in the gradient once they are sampled. When a correct low-confidence trajectory appears, it is still reinforced with a positive update proportional to $\hat A_i \hat c_i \hat d_q$, especially on hard questions. In our difficulty-stratified experiments, CoDaPO improves performance more on the hardest levels than on the easiest ones, which is consistent with rare hard successes being reinforced rather than suppressed.

In the revision, we will (i) add a short explanation in Section 4 that explicitly orders the effective updates for correct high confidence, correct low confidence, incorrect high confidence, and incorrect low confidence trajectories; (ii) include a small quantitative analysis comparing the fraction of gradient mass coming from correct low confidence trajectories under GRPO and CoDaPO, especially on hard questions; and (iii) clarify in the text that CoDaPO leaves the sampling policy unchanged and only reweights gradients, so exploration and rare discoveries remain intact.

summary.value: This paper does an empirical analysis of GRPO (or more precisely, a variant of it called DAPO), through the lens of model miscalibration during training on MATH, and disentangling across 5 levels of difficulty of problems.

strengths.value:
The main strengths of the paper are:
- the empirical analysis of the authors is solid and their findings are reasonable - particularly, I found interesting the beginning of section 3.2 on miscalibration 
- the authors find that applying the same advantage for every token is detrimental for learning, which makes sense given that there are probably few tokens that actually matter for the solution and many filler ones, especially in math proofs (such as "thus", "therefore" etc)

While the analysis is interesting, I believe there are several major weaknesses with the paper which I present below.

weaknesses.value:
- To begin, it would be good if the authors would give quantitative analysis of the distributions in figure 2 and 3 (namely, min, max, mean, median and kurtosis) since currently it is quite hard to verify qualitatively the statements about tails in Section 3.3

- My second major issue with the current paper is that it does not appear that CoDaPO improves over the baselines (DAPO, and GRPO) in Table 2. Concretely, the improvements are at most 2%, which in general is not statistically significant for post training due the RL noise. Moreover, as far as I understand, the current comparison does not sweep over hyperparameters, and thus it is even more unclear whether the proposed would have any benefit at all under a well tuned baseline.

As a meta comment, while I think the empirical analysis is quite solid and interesting, the paper would be better framed as a science paper studying GRPO rather than proposing a new method which as it stands does not bring any improvements over existing algorithms. Due to this, I am inclined to reject this work.

### Q6. Training on other model families.
> Reviewer rMTD: Would it be possible to try CoDAPO on another family of base model, not Qwen (eg. OctoThinker from Llama3.1-8B [1])?

**Reply:** Thank you for this suggestion. **In brief, CoDaPO is not tied to the Qwen family, and we have already run it on a non-Qwen base model (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) under the same post-training setup**. On this backbone, CoDaPO again outperforms GRPO and DAPO, which supports that our method generalizes beyond Qwen; applying it to larger Llama-based mid-training models such as OctoThinker is a natural but resource-intensive next step.

**(1) CoDaPO is architecture agnostic and only modifies GRPO’s weighting, not the backbone.** The CoDaPO update replaces the GRPO weight with $w^{\text{CoDaPO}}\_{i,t} = \tilde{\rho}\_{i,t}\hat{A}_i\hat{c}_i\hat{d}_q$, where $\hat{c}_i$ and $\hat{d}_q$ depend on trajectory-level confidence and question-level difficulty. This construction does not assume any Qwen-specific architecture, tokenizer, or pretraining; it only requires a GRPO-style RL loop with group-normalized advantages. In principle it can be applied to Qwen, Llama, or any decoder-only transformer trained with GRPO or similar objectives.

**(2) We have evaluated CoDaPO on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and see consistent gains over all GRPO-style baselines.** To test cross-family generalization, we repeated our post-training pipeline on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, using the same datasets, reward, group size, sampling strategy, and training budget as in the Qwen experiments. On this Llama model, CoDaPO achieves the best average performance across the math benchmarks, improving over GRPO and DAPO by margins similar to those in the Qwen results. We also observe qualitatively similar PRAG dynamics (for example, advantage contraction under vanilla GRPO and their mitigation under CoDaPO), which indicates that CoDaPO is acting on general properties of the GRPO update rather than on Qwen-specific quirks.

The confidence used in Figures 2 and 4 is then defined as $\text{Conf}(q, o_i) = \exp(\bar{\ell}_i) = \left(\prod\_{t=1}^{|o_i|} f\_\theta(o\_{i,t} \mid q, o\_{i,<t})\right)^{1 / |o_i|}$, which is the geometric mean of the token probabilities. Since each token probability is in $[0, 1]$, their geometric mean is also in $[0, 1]$, which explains the range on the horizontal axis.

**(2) Mean log probability is the underlying signal; exponentiation is only for interpretability and does not change the analysis.** In the text we refer to “mean log probability” as the confidence statistic, meaning $\bar{\ell}_i$. For plotting and for a more intuitive scale, we apply the monotone transformation $\exp(\cdot)$ and display $\text{Conf}(q, o_i) = \exp(\bar{\ell}_i)$ in $[0, 1]$. Because the exponential is strictly increasing, ranking trajectories by $\bar{\ell}_i$ or by $\text{Conf}(q, o_i)$ is equivalent, so none of the conclusions about confidence or calibration depend on this choice; it is purely a visualization normalization.

In the revision, we will explicitly define $\text{Conf}(q, o_i) = \exp\big(\frac{1}{|o_i|} \sum_t \log f_\theta(o\_{i,t} \mid q, o\_{i,<t})\big)$ when confidence is first introduced, update the captions of Figures 2 and 4 to state that the x axis is the geometric mean token probability, and adjust the surrounding wording so the normalization from mean log probability to $[0, 1]$ is immediately clear.

In brief, Eq. 12 is intended to define a group normalized confidence weight $c_i$ (and a question level difficulty weight $d_q$) that directly rescales advantages, rather than an entropy loss. In the following, we elaborate on how these quantities are calculated and why such weighting brings practical benefits.

**(1) Regarding the confidence term $c_i$**, our goal is to dynamically adjust the advantage weight of each response during training based on the model’s confidence in that response in order to facilitate learning. The detailed computation in Eq. 12 is: for each trajectory $o_i$ in a group of size $G$, we first define its average log probability $\bar{\ell}_i = \frac{1}{|o_i|} \sum_t \log f\_\theta(o\_{i,t} \mid q, o\_{i,<t}),$ and the group average $\bar{\ell}_q = \frac{1}{G} \sum\_{j=1}^G \bar{\ell}_j.$ We then set $c_i = \sigma\left(\frac{\bar{\ell}_q}{\bar{\ell}_i}\right),$ where $\sigma$ is a sigmoid.

**The purpose of $c_i$ is to rank and reweight trajectories by relative confidence within a group, not to add a global entropy loss.** Our goal is to change which trajectories dominate the gradient for a fixed question $q$. We want: (i) among correct trajectories, more confident ones to receive larger positive effective advantages; (ii) among incorrect trajectories, more confident ones to receive larger negative penalties. Since log probabilities are non-positive, a trajectory with higher confidence has $\bar{\ell}_i$ closer to 0 than the group average $\bar{\ell}_q$, so the ratio $\bar{\ell}_q / \bar{\ell}_i$ is greater than 1 and $c_i$ increases after the sigmoid. Multiplying $c_i$ by the normalized advantage $\hat{A}_i$ in $g\_{i,t} \propto \hat{A}_i c_i d_q \rho\_{i,t} \nabla\_\theta \ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t})$ then yields exactly the desired effect: high confidence correct trajectories get the largest positive updates, and high confidence incorrect trajectories get the largest negative updates, with all weights bounded by the sigmoid.

Specifically, we observe a dual-mode learning trend during GRPO training: 1) Simple problems (e.g., Level 1) converge quickly with high accuracy. 2) Hard problems (e.g., Level 5) also show some improvement but retain a significant proportion of errors. At this stage, further improving model performance requires boosting accuracy on hard problems without sacrificing accuracy on easy ones. 

**To this end, we introduce a U-shaped difficulty weight $d_q$ with respect to the group correctness rate $\bar{r}_q = \frac{1}{G} \sum_i r_i(q)$, emphasizing both ends of the difficulty spectrum.** Both very easy and very hard questions receive larger total gradient mass, while medium questions receive less. Intuitively, for easy questions, $d_q$ magnifies penalties on the remaining mistakes, and for hard questions, it amplifies reinforcement on rare correct trajectories. The benefit of this design is two-fold: 1) For easy problems, it penalizes incorrect responses more strongly, since correct responses already yield near-zero advantage; 2) For hard problems, it rewards correct responses more effectively, as incorrect responses tend to have near-zero advantage.

In contrast, $c_i$ is applied directly to $\hat{A}_i$, so the gradient depends on both confidence and correctness: high confidence wrong answers receive stronger negative updates, high confidence correct answers receive stronger positive updates, and low confidence examples are de-emphasized. >### W2. Include additional analyses on the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm compared with baseline methods.

**Reply:** Thank you for this helpful suggestion. **In brief, CoDaPO is designed to have essentially the same computational cost as GRPO, because it reuses quantities that GRPO already computes and only adds inexpensive scalar operations.**

The confidence factor $\hat{c}_i$ is a smooth function of the trajectory log probability $\ell\_i = \frac{1}{|o_i|}\sum_t \log f\_\theta(o\_{i,t}\mid q,o\_{i,<t})$, which is already available when forming the importance ratios. The difficulty factor $\hat{d}_q$ is a function of per-question correctness, computed from rewards $r_i$ that are already used to build advantages. Thus, CoDaPO only performs extra averaging, normalization, and a sigmoid or simple polynomial on existing tensors, without invoking any additional model evaluations or backward passes.

**(2) In practice, runtime and memory usage are effectively identical to GRPO under the same configuration.** Because all additional work in CoDaPO consists of lightweight elementwise operations on per-trajectory scalars, the dominant cost remains the transformer forward and backward passes, as in GRPO and DAPO. In our implementation, when we run GRPO and CoDaPO with the same model, batch size, sequence length, and group size, step time and peak GPU memory differ only within measurement noise. There is no extra sampling, no auxiliary network, and no enlarged computation graph that would materially change throughput or memory.

**(3) Compared to more elaborate GRPO variants, CoDaPO remains a lightweight, drop-in modification.** Methods such as DAPO introduce additional mechanisms like dynamic resampling or modified clipping that can complicate the training pipeline. CoDaPO instead operates purely at the objective level: it replaces the scalar multiplier on $\hat{A}_i$ with $\hat{c}_i \hat{d}_q$ and leaves the rest of the GRPO loop unchanged. This makes it easy to integrate into existing GRPO style codebases and to combine with other variants, while keeping computational requirements on par with the original method.

In the revision, we will (i) add a short subsection explicitly explaining that $\hat{c}_i$ and $\hat{d}_q$ are computed from intermediate quantities that GRPO already produces, and (ii) emphasize in the experimental setup that CoDaPO is a computationally cheap, drop-in replacement for the GRPO surrogate.

>### W2. The effect of the difficulty weight is not significant.

**Reply:** Thank you for the thoughtful comment. **Regarding the reweighting mechanism, we would like to clarify the potential misunderstanding in your review.**

In brief, our difficulty term does not try to make the model uniformly more confident on easy or hard examples; instead, it reweights gradient contributions within each difficulty bucket so that overconfident errors on easy questions are penalized and rare correct reasoning on hard questions is amplified. This explains why Figure 4 does not show a dramatically different marginal confidence or entropy pattern. Our design is also conceptually different from priority sampling in Kimi 1.5, and we clarify this connection and add supporting experiments and analysis in the revision.

**(1) The difficulty term reweights gradient contributions within each difficulty group rather than enforcing higher confidence on all easy or hard samples.** In CoDaPO, the trajectory level weight can be written as $w_i \propto \hat{A}_i \hat{c}_i \hat{d}_q,$ or at the token level $w^{\text{CoDaPO}}\_{i,t} = \rho\_{i,t} \hat{A}_i \hat{c}_i \hat{d}_q,$ where $\hat{A}_i$ is the normalized advantage, $\hat{c}_i$ is the confidence factor, and $\hat{d}_q$ is the difficulty factor for question $q$ computed from the group correctness rate $\bar r_q$. Crucially, $\hat{d}_q$ multiplies both positive and negative advantages. 

For easy questions (high $\bar r_q$), most trajectories are correct, so the largest magnitude advantages come from the few incorrect, often high-confidence, responses with large negative $\hat{A}_i$. Increasing $\hat{d}_q$ in this regime magnifies the penalty on these overconfident mistakes rather than pushing correct responses to even higher confidence. 

For hard questions (low $\bar r_q$), most trajectories are incorrect with small or clipped negative advantages, and the rare correct trajectories carry large positive $\hat{A}_i$. Here, a larger $\hat{d}_q$ amplifies the positive reinforcement on these emerging correct solutions. Thus, the difficulty term emphasizes the most informative gradients within each difficulty group instead of enforcing uniformly higher confidence on all easy or hard samples.

summary.value: The paper defines and analyzes three existing problems in the existing GRPO mechanism and proposes an optimization algorithm, CoDaPO, targeting to address these problems by embedding the notion of model confidence and problem difficulty into the optimization objective. CoDaPO demonstrates improvement over alternative optimization methods on average in a suite of mathematical reasoning benchmarks on the 1.5B and 7B scale Qwen models. The paper also includes a set of ablation studies on the component of CoDaPO.

- The paper clearly identifies the existing problems in GPRO in formal analyses, highlighting the motivation of their method very well.
- The paper formally shows how the introduction of confidence and difficulty would address these problems, making the design choices of method convincing.
- The paper provides a good amount of illustrations that are helpful in understanding the analysis and the impact of CoDaPO intuitively.

>### Q2. Changes in Section 3 when training purely on-policy.

**Reply:** Thank you for this thoughtful question. In short, Section 3 is explicitly analyzing the standard GRPO regime with clipped ratios and mildly off-policy updates, where the combination of clipping and $\rho\_{i,t}$ produces a one-way probability drift and entropy collapse. **If clipping were removed or if training were made strictly on policy with $\rho\_{i,t}=1$, that specific asymmetric mechanism would largely disappear, while other phenomena like advantage contraction would remain.**

**(1) The one-way drift in Section 3.2 comes from asymmetric clipping in the off-policy setting.** In our GRPO analysis, the token-level policy update (ignoring KL for brevity) can be written as $\Delta \ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t}) \propto \mathbf{1}\_{\text{unclipped}(i,t)} \hat A_i \rho\_{i,t}$, where $\hat A_i$ is the group normalized advantage, $\rho\_{i,t} = \frac{f\_{\theta}(o\_{i,t}\mid q, o\_{i,<t})}{f\_{\text{old}}(o\_{i,t}\mid q, o\_{i,<t})}$, and $\mathbf{1}\_{\text{unclipped}}$ indicates that $\rho\_{i,t}$ is within $[1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]$. For $\hat A_i > 0$, updates keep increasing $\ell\_\theta$ until $\rho\_{i,t}$ hits $1+\epsilon$. For $\hat A_i < 0$, once $\rho\_{i,t} < 1-\epsilon$, the clipped branch becomes constant and the negative update shuts off. This asymmetry is what drives the one-way upward drift and entropy collapse we highlight in Section 3.2.

**(2) Removing clipping would remove this truncation but increase variance and potential instability.** If clipping is removed and the surrogate uses the unclipped term $\rho\_{i,t}\hat A_i$ everywhere, then both positive and negative advantages continue to contribute $\Delta \ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t}) \propto \rho\_{i,t}\hat A_i$ with no regime in which negative advantage trajectories are frozen. The specific clipping-induced one-way drift would no longer occur, and we would expect less mechanically driven entropy collapse and more symmetric probability updates. However, large or small $\rho\_{i,t}$ would then produce unbounded gradients, increasing variance and the risk of unstable training, especially when the policy moves far from $f\_{\text{old}}$.

**(3) In the purely on policy case with $\rho\_{i,t}=1$, the clipping asymmetry also disappears and the gradient becomes symmetric in $\hat A_i$.** If rollouts are generated strictly under the current policy and we take $\rho\_{i,t} = 1$ for all tokens, then in the unclipped region the policy term reduces to $\Delta \ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t}) \propto \hat A_i$, and the clipped surrogate degenerates to the usual on-policy policy gradient. The min operation never produces an asymmetric “shut off” of negative advantage trajectories, so the one-way drift mechanism is absent. Entropy can still decrease because correct trajectories tend to have positive $\hat A_i$, but this is no longer driven by structural asymmetry in $\rho\_{i,t}$ and clipping. In this regime, our results on probability drift and entropy collapse from clipping would not apply, while our observations about group normalization and difficulty (advantage contraction and hierarchical convergence) would still hold, since they depend on how $\hat A_i$ is constructed rather than on clipping.

**(4) Our analysis and experiments focus on the clipped, mildly off-policy GRPO regime used in practice.** The GRPO runs we study in Sections 3–5 use the standard PPO style setup: trajectories are sampled from a slightly lagged policy $f\_{\text{old}}$, we apply clipping with $\epsilon$, and we reuse each batch for a small number of epochs. This is exactly the regime where we empirically observe probability inflation, entropy collapse, advantage contraction, and hierarchical convergence, and where the asymmetric truncation mechanism is most relevant. CoDaPO is designed as a modification of this practical GRPO setting, not as a proposal for fully unclipped or purely on-policy training.

In the revision, we will (i) explicitly state in Section 3.2 that the one-way drift analysis assumes clipped ratios with $\rho\_{i,t}$ computed under $f\_{\text{old}}$, (ii) add a short discussion of how the conclusions change in the hypothetical unclipped and strictly on-policy cases, and (iii) if space and compute permit, include an ablation (in the appendix) that either removes clipping or makes updates more on policy and reports the corresponding PRAG diagnostics to empirically support this discussion.

**Reply:** Thank you for this thoughtful observation. 

In brief, Table 2 shows that (i) both confidence and difficulty reweighting individually give clear gains over GRPO; (ii) their small gap on MATH500 reflects overlapping effects on a single aggregate metric rather than redundancy; and (iii) they remain conceptually complementary in how they reshape gradients, which we will make clearer with additional analyses. 

**(1) The main gain in performance comes from moving from plain GRPO to the PRAG-guided reweighting.** In Table 2, both GRPO + confidence only and GRPO + difficulty only significantly improve over vanilla GRPO on MATH500, while full CoDaPO (both terms) is best. Our Section 3 is explicitly an analysis of GRPO, not a new algorithm that ignores KL. CoDaPO is then obtained by modifying the advantage weighting and micro averaging and by operating in the $\beta = 0$ regime. Showing the full GRPO objective, including KL, makes it clear what is being changed and why.

(6) is intended as a precise characterization of the KL gradient, and we will present it more formally and concisely.** At the token level, if $\ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t}) = f_\theta(o\_{i,t}\mid q,o\_{i,<t})$ and $\ell\_{\text{ref}}(o\_{i,t}) = f\_{\text{ref}}(o\_{i,t}\mid q,o\_{i,<t})$, the KL term contributes $\nabla_\theta{\ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t})}\big[\beta \mathrm{KL}(f_\theta || f\_{\text{ref}})\big] = \beta\big(1 - u\_{i,t}\big),$ where $u\_{i,t} = \frac{\ell\_{\text{ref}}(o\_{i,t})}{\ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t})}$. This is exactly the $-\beta(1 - u\_{i,t})$ term in Eq. (6) with the opposite sign in the update. From this, one directly obtains $-\beta(1 - u\_{i,t}) < 0$ if $\ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t}) > \ell\_{\text{ref}}(o\_{i,t}),$ and $-\beta(1 - u\_{i,t}) > 0$ if $\ell\_\theta(o\_{i,t}) < \ell\_{\text{ref}}(o\_{i,t})$. So KL always pulls $f_\theta$ toward $f\_{\text{ref}}$. The key point is that this symmetric pull contrasts with the asymmetric clipping term that mainly pushes probabilities upward on high-advantage trajectories. In the revision, we will state this gradient result cleanly and move algebraic details to the appendix so it does not feel informal or overlong.
